title: Deriving kinetic energy
prior_knowledge_summary: Work done by a constant force along a displacement is W = Fs.
Newton's second law can be written as F = ma for a constant resultant force.
For constant acceleration, v^2 = u^2 + 2as links speed and displacement without time.
new_learning: Connect work done by a resultant force to a change in kinetic energy.
Derive Delta E_K = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2) for constant acceleration.
Obtain E_K = 1/2 mv^2 by choosing rest as the zero-kinetic-energy state.
Use units and limiting cases to check the derived expression.

visual_planning.reason: Six planned figures separate the physical story, algebraic substitutions, comparison, checking and synthesis. No image assets were created in this four-file task.
visual_planning.style: rectangular white-paper colourful hand-drawn teacher sketch

blocks.title: Why does speed appear squared?
content: A small trolley and a heavy trolley can move at the same speed, yet the heavy trolley is harder to stop. A single trolley moving twice as fast is also harder to stop, but not merely twice as hard.
Predict this: if the speed doubles while mass stays fixed, does the energy of motion double or become four times as large? We need a derivation because a guess from everyday feeling is unreliable.

figure.purpose: Create the opening comparison between mass, speed and stopping work
figure.brief: Landscape teacher sketch with three trolleys on straight tracks: one light at speed v, one heavier at speed v, and one light at speed 2v. Show equal braking-force arrows and leave stopping-distance outcomes as question marks.
figure.alt_text: Three trolleys compare changed mass and changed speed while braking-force arrows are equal.

blocks.title: Work transfers energy into motion
content: The controlled definition of work done is: product of force and displacement in the direction of the force. Its controlled ID is 9702_def_work_done.
For a constant resultant force along the displacement, remember W = Fs. Here W is work done in joules, F is resultant force in newtons and s is displacement in metres.

When this resultant force speeds up an object and no other energy store is involved, the work done is the increase in kinetic energy. Work is the transfer, while kinetic energy is the energy the moving object has.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: product of force and displacement in the direction of the force

figure.purpose: Distinguish energy transfer by work from stored kinetic energy
figure.brief: A left-to-right causal strip: resultant force acts through displacement, work is done, speed rises, kinetic energy rises. Use separate arrows for force and motion and no final formula.
figure.alt_text: A causal strip links force through displacement to work done and increased kinetic energy.

blocks.title: Replace force and displacement with motion quantities
content: Start with W = Fs. The force is a resultant force, so Newton's second law gives F = ma. Substitution gives W = mas.
Now use the constant-acceleration formula v^2 = u^2 + 2as. Rearranging gives as = (v^2 - u^2) / 2.

Substitute this whole expression for as: W = m(v^2 - u^2) / 2 = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2). The acceleration disappears because a smaller acceleration acts through a larger displacement to produce the same change of speed.

figure.purpose: Make the two substitutions and cancellation visible
figure.brief: Annotated algebra flow with W = Fs at the top, F replaced by ma on the left branch, as replaced by (v squared minus u squared) over 2 on the right branch, then both branches meet at W = one half m times (v squared minus u squared).
figure.alt_text: An algebra flow shows how force and displacement substitutions lead to the change in kinetic energy.

blocks.title: From a change in energy to the kinetic-energy formula
content: The result W = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2) describes an energy change. It can be written as Delta E_K = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2).
Choose the object at rest as the zero-kinetic-energy state. Then u = 0 and the final speed is v. The expression becomes E_K = 1/2 m(v^2 - 0^2) = 1/2 mv^2.
The controlled definition of kinetic energy is: energy that an object has because of its motion. Its controlled ID is 9702_def_kinetic_energy.
Remember E_K = 1/2 mv^2. E_K is measured in joules, m in kilograms and v in metres per second.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: energy that an object has because of its motion

figure.purpose: Show why setting the initial speed to zero produces the stored-energy expression
figure.brief: Two-state sketch of one trolley: rest state labelled u = 0 and moving state labelled v, with a work-transfer arrow between them. Place Delta E_K beneath the pair and E_K beneath the moving state.
figure.alt_text: A trolley changes from rest to speed v, connecting work done to its final kinetic energy.

blocks.title: Two complete numerical checks
content: A 10 kg practice sled speeds up from 2.0 m s^-1 to 6.0 m s^-1. Delta E_K = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2) = 1/2 x 10 x (6.0^2 - 2.0^2) = 5 x (36 - 4) = 160 J.
The initial kinetic energy is 1/2 x 10 x 2.0^2 = 20 J. The final kinetic energy is 1/2 x 10 x 6.0^2 = 180 J. Their difference is 180 J - 20 J = 160 J, matching the direct change formula.

Now check the connection to motion by a different route. A 5.0 kg trolley moving at 2.0 m s^-1 is pushed by a constant resultant force of 10 N through 6.0 m. The work is 60 J, so its final kinetic energy is 10 J + 60 J = 70 J. From 1/2 x 5.0 x v^2 = 70, v^2 = 28 m^2 s^-2.
Independently, a = F/m = 2.0 m s^-2 and v^2 = u^2 + 2as = 2.0^2 + 2 x 2.0 x 6.0 = 28 m^2 s^-2. Both routes agree. A unit check also works because kg m^2 s^-2 is a joule.

figure.purpose: Compare energy-difference and motion-equation checks without repeating a practice question
figure.brief: Split worked layout. The upper row compares a direct energy-change calculation with final energy minus initial energy for the sled, meeting at 160 J. The lower row compares work-energy and constant-acceleration routes for the trolley, meeting at v squared equals 28 metres squared per second squared.
figure.alt_text: Two worked checks compare independent routes to the same energy change and final speed.

blocks.title: Twice the speed does not mean twice the kinetic energy
content: It feels natural to expect energy to follow speed directly because twice the speed sounds like twice the motion. The derivation shows where that intuition fails: displacement under constant acceleration brings in v^2, not v.
For fixed mass, replacing v by 2v gives E_K = 1/2 m(2v)^2 = 4(1/2 mv^2). Doubling speed makes kinetic energy four times as large. Doubling mass at fixed speed only doubles kinetic energy.
The formula also passes a limiting check. If v = 0, then E_K = 0. Kinetic energy cannot be negative because mass is positive and speed is squared.

figure.purpose: Correct linear-speed intuition with a proportional comparison
figure.brief: Comparison table for the same mass at speeds v and 2v, with speed bars of lengths 1 and 2 and kinetic-energy blocks of areas 1 and 4. Add a separate row showing double mass at fixed speed gives double energy.
figure.alt_text: A comparison shows that doubling speed quadruples kinetic energy while doubling mass doubles it.

blocks.title: The derivation in one connected chain
content: Start from W = Fs. Replace F by ma. Replace as using v^2 = u^2 + 2as. This gives W = 1/2 m(v^2 - u^2).
Interpret work by the resultant force as the change in kinetic energy. If the object starts from rest, u = 0, so E_K = 1/2 mv^2.

Keep the assumptions visible: the force is the resultant force, it is constant and along the displacement, and the motion has constant acceleration. The final energy formula remains valid beyond this simple derivation, but these assumptions make the derivation possible with the equations available here.
